headline: This man's testosterone
punch: At 28 his growth plates were still wide open.

headline: Everyone credits
body: It's the hormone people associate with male puberty, male bone, male height. So the assumption is that it's also what ends your growth.
punch: The assumption is wrong — and one patient proved it.

headline: The patient
body: A 28-year-old man carried a mutation that broke his estrogen receptor. His testosterone was normal, even slightly high. He was fully masculinised. Everything androgen-driven worked exactly as it should.
punch: His epiphyses never fused and he kept growing linearly into adulthood.

headline: And here's the control
body: He was given estrogen therapy for six months. His free estradiol rose roughly tenfold. Nothing happened — no bone response at all, because the receptor reading the signal was broken.
punch: The hormone was present. The receiver wasn't. The plates stayed open.

headline: Which means
body: Androgens get converted into estrogen by aromatase — including inside growth plate cartilage itself. Testosterone doesn't close your plates directly. It gets turned into the thing that does.
punch: Cartilage isn't a passive target. It makes its own estrogen locally.

headline: And it works in reverse
body: Block aromatase with letrozole or anastrozole in boys and bone maturation slows and adult height increases. That's the hypothesis tested forward, in humans, with a real endpoint.
punch: Blocking the conversion delays the closure. Every time.

headline: But don't oversimplify it
body: Block the estrogen receptor entirely with fulvestrant in mice — no ER signalling at all, aromatisation irrelevant — and testosterone still accelerates skeletal maturation.
punch: Something androgen-driven is happening that estrogen can't explain.

headline: There's also a third
body: GPER-1 does roughly the opposite of ERα: it promotes chondrocyte proliferation and delays hypertrophy. Its expression peaks early in puberty, then falls as classical estrogen signalling rises.
punch: Estrogen may switch from pro-growth to pro-closure as puberty runs.

headline: So the honest version
body: Estrogen is the dominant lever on growth plate closure — that part is settled by human genetics and clinical trials. Whether androgens also act directly is still genuinely contested.
punch: Anyone giving you one clean sentence is skipping the argument.

headline: It's never over
body: Real mechanisms, real citations, no protocols.
